body:
A shoulder injury kept him out of the Texas upset, but the junior is back under center against No. 3 Georgia in a pivotal Atlanta rivalry clash
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 30, 2026

        Aaron Philo will return and start at quarterback for Florida against Georgia for a crucial SEC showdown Saturday in Atlanta, a source familiar with the decision told CBS Sports.The junior returns after a shoulder injury kept him on the sideline of the Gators' 27-24 upset of then-No. 7 Texas two weeks ago. Tramell Jones Jr., who started against Texas, will be available Saturday.Philo was hurt in Florida's 38-19 homecoming loss to South Carolina on Oct. 10. A week later in Austin, he was available only in an emergency role, and coach Jon Sumrall kept him on the sideline.Jones completed 22 of 35 passes for 155 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions in his first career start against the Longhorns. 
Both quarterbacks are battling injuries and were listed as questionable Thursday on the SEC's player availability report.Sumrall said there would be no formal announcement on a starter before the game.The game feels like a homecoming for Philo. He led Prince Avenue Christian, near Athens, to consecutive state titles and broke Georgia's all-time high school passing record, held by former Clemson quarterback Trevor Lawrence. Philo didn't play in either of Georgia Tech's losses to Georgia during his career in Atlanta.  Philo started Florida's first six games, completing 70.5% of his passes for 1,341 yards and nine touchdowns with three interceptions. Philo transferred from Georgia Tech, following offensive coordinator Buster Faulkner to Gainesville, where he beat Jones in preseason competition for the job.
The No. 17 Gators (5-2, 3-2 SEC) climbed as high as No. 8 in the polls after starting 4-0, highlighted by a 52-28 win against then-No. 4 Ole Miss in The Swamp. Then the Gators lost back-to-back games in October, a 45-17 loss at Missouri and a 38-19 loss at home to unranked South Carolina.The CBS Sports CFP Forecaster gives Florida a 9.5% chance to make the field. An upset of No. 3 Georgia (6-1, 4-1) would push that to 29%.Georgia is coming off a home loss to Auburn on a last-second field goal. The Bulldogs rested and recouped during a bye week following the 27-24 defeat. Georgia leads the SEC in scoring defense (15.9) and remains one of two teams (Kentucky) with only one loss in the SEC. 
Kickoff Saturday is scheduled for 3:30 p.m. ET on ABC at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. It's the first time the rivalry will be played in Atlanta. The traditional venue, EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, is undergoing renovations.

title: Why Man City's complaints about the 'Red Cartel' ring hollow - CBS Sports

body:
As two of their number face off at Anfield on Sunday afternoon, this would seem to be a good time to find yourself one of the so-called Red Cartel. Manchester City are facing the prospect of sanctions that would cast them out from the Premier League's inner circle, while those other big-six clubs that play in white and blue have spent half a decade retreating from the title race (as, it should be noted, have Manchester United).If City's sanctions land this season, it could be that Liverpool are the nearest rivals to Arsenal in the title race, another domestic crown carved up by the grand old dukes of the English game. Believe City's defenders and this triopoly is just what Abu Dhabi protected the Premier League from. "A conspiracy by the Red Cartel to keep clubs like Manchester City out of sitting at the top table," was how one supporter described the finding that City had breached 114 of the Premier League's rules over a nine-season period. When their chief executive Ferran Soriano talks about a "Premier League conspiracy theory," well, no one thinks the shadowy cabal is being led by Brentford and Bournemouth.A version of this framing has gathered pace beyond the realms of the Etihad Stadium, intermingling with burgeoning dissatisfaction over financial rules from both the Premier League and UEFA, that have resulted in sanctions for grand old clubs such as Everton, Nottingham Forest and Aston Villa. It was best articulated by ex-Chelsea midfielder Joe Cole earlier this month, who insisted that the game's financial settlement was locking out ambitious clubs in a way that his former club was not when it was bought by Roman Abramovich."The regulations that are in place are not doing the job they're supposed to do," he said. Of course, there is one crucial caveat to any assessment of the Premier League's profit and sustainability regulations (PSR) and the squad cost ratio that has replaced it. When one team is found to have flouted them through "sham" contracts that inflated its revenue to the tune of over $1 billion, it is quite hard to know how this sport might operate on a level playing field. Under Pep Guardiola, City's domestic achievements were unprecedented. No English side had sustained a four-year spell of domestic preeminence, won all three domestic trophies or delivered a 100-point season.
Anyone who argues that, were it not for City, this would have been a Premier League dominated by the big boys in red must accept that they are engaged in historical counterfactuals. What actually happened was a record-breaking spell of dominance by a team that, it was found, "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade."Were City really a bulwark against the cartel?Then again, if you were to journey through the what-ifs, maybes and never-weres of the last 18 years, you would struggle to immediately and convincingly argue that it was City and City alone who stood against the LaLiga-fication of the Premier League. Indeed, there was never really a period when all three of Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United were in the chasing pack.  The last season in which these teams all finished in the Premier League top four was 2008-09, the campaign whose defining moment was the unheralded sale of City to Sheikh Mansour on Sept. 1. Indeed, 2026-27 should be considered a banner year in the smoke-filled, oak-clad boardrooms of the cartel. For the first time since 2009-10, all three of their teams are playing in the Champions League.  The intervening 17 years had their ups and downs for all three: a pair of eighth-placed finishes each for Arsenal and Liverpool, that 15th place for Manchester United and whatever they have themselves on course for this time out. One or two have generally been there or thereabouts, but all three at once just has not happened. Nor did it really happen before the Manchester City takeover.
                                                                    CBS Sports
                                                            The period between 1996 and 2009 is the exception to the rule, containing 10 of the 11 seasons in which Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have all occupied top-four positions. Either side of that, you have broad similarities. The late 1950s and early 1960s is the only period in English footballing history when none of the triumvirate was in the top four, and the turn of the millennium the only one when all three were.
The mid-2000s was also perhaps the era when the Premier League's most successful sides had the most meaningful financial heft when compared to the rest of the English game. In the year before the takeover at what was then the City of Manchester Stadium, Manchester United posted revenues of €324.8 million, making them the second-richest club in Europe behind Real Madrid.At that time, the seventh-richest club in England was, ironically, Manchester City. Their €104 million in earnings was barely enough to place them in the Deloitte Money League outright. In 20th place, they were being out-earned not only by the boys in red but also by the likes of Fenerbahce, VfB Stuttgart and Olympique de Marseille. The gap between them and England's monied elite was vast, United raking in more than three times the revenue of their noisy neighbors.Move on to the most recent Money League and the picture has changed more significantly than it might initially appear. In 2024-25, the richest club in England still played in red, Liverpool taking in €836.1 million in their title-winning season. This time, however, the seventh-richest English side, Aston Villa, had earned €450.2 million.
In absolute terms, of course, the gap is far greater, but what matters more is the proportions. In 2008, the seventh-richest team in England earned less than a third of what the richest did. Seventeen years later, the richest earns less than double. Meanwhile, the comparative purchasing power of any Premier League side has risen. Nine of the 20 richest clubs in the game are English, as are half of the top 30. Two decades ago, it would have been unimaginable that a club like Brentford might snare Mamadou Sangare from the runners-up in Ligue 1, that Bournemouth might pick up future stars like Junior Kroupi and Antonio Silva, and that a newly promoted side like Ipswich might have the finances to land a Bundesliga champion in Exequiel Palacios.As football finance expert Kieran Maguire puts it, "the Premier League is the Super League." Scarcely a week goes by without it being impressed on Manchester United that they cannot spend their way out of their latest crisis. It is perhaps too early to be certain what this all means, but it is worth noting that in the past four seasons Bournemouth, Aston Villa, Newcastle (unable to turn on the money taps like City were when they were taken over by sovereign wealth) and Brighton have all broken into the top six.  If the gravitational pull of talent to the Premier League remains as is, an era of relative competitiveness seems plausible. Meanwhile, supporters of West Ham, Villa and Crystal Palace are discovering that a domestic cup win or a strong Premier League campaign can be parlayed into the sorts of European nights they will never forget.This is not the 1950s or 1960s anymore, when provincial clubs from across the land could take a big swing at a title, but imagine a world where the regulations that Cole and others bemoan were struck from the books. Nothing would stand in the way of those with sovereign-wealth money -- Newcastle United and Manchester City -- but themselves. Those other ambitious clubs that just want to spend their owners' cash could soon find themselves dicing with danger. PSR and UEFA's financial fair play regulations would appear to have entrenched the old powers, but in the last decade and a half no Premier League side with dreams of grandeur has taken the route to the precipice of oblivion that Leeds United and Portsmouth did.
The Big PictureThe arc of the Premier League itself might be very slowly bending toward parity, but that does not mean that Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal are necessarily happy with the status quo. Indeed, if there is any justification for the conspiratorial thinking of City supporters, it comes in how their rivals have attempted to change the playing field to suit their needs.In October 2020, the owners of Liverpool and Manchester United proposed Project Big Picture, offering the lower leagues a financial life raft in the form of an immediate $325 million payment and a 25% cut of future Premier League TV deals. That came with strings attached, the most notable being a shrinking of the calendar that would surely have suited those teams with lucrative Champions League fixtures and preseason tours. Nine clubs would also have been afforded special voting rights, Liverpool, Manchester United, Arsenal (and City) among them.A little over six months later came proposals for a European Super League. Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham were in on this one, but it was notable that three of the league's five founders were Joel Glazer (co-owner of Manchester United), John W. Henry (owner of Liverpool) and Stan Kroenke (owner of Arsenal).
"There has been a broad attempt to change the landscape," says Maguire. "Kroenke, Henry and the Glazers are likely to have broadly similar views to each other. Conceptually there is no doubt that what they would like from football going forwards [is greater influence and revenue]. Spurs would like to be at the table with them. Chelsea under Clearlake Capital, the same. Under Abramovich, I'm not sure it would be the same. 
        
            
                Manchester City's 'sliding doors' moment: How the Premier League changed after Abu Dhabi started spending
                
                    James Benge                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
"Manchester City were quite happy being Manchester City. They were quite prepared to achieve what they wanted to independently, as we now find, through sham contracts."If that all sounds quite cartel-ish, Maguire would suggest otherwise. "A cartel stops everybody else from taking part. This is an interest group who have common interest. They're trying to hijack the legacy sport of football for their own ends."
Their past wheezes may have fallen foul of the English supporter, but Maguire predicts they will try again, pointing to the increasingly likely re-election of Gianni Infantino as FIFA president next March. That could mean a doubling down on the Club World Cup, for which a joint venture has been agreed with European Football Clubs. It is expected that the 2029 iteration of the competition will make room for more clubs per country, opening the door for at least some of the Premier League's red brigade (unfortunately for Manchester United, qualifying for any global competition on sporting merit seems a long shot)."Those clubs will want to ensure that they're at the top [of the] table because Chelsea made £80 million from winning a competition last year that nobody watched," says Maguire. "They will watch if we've got four Spanish teams, four English teams and so on as opposed to the two of the latter. It would have helped if it had been Manchester United and Liverpool, as opposed to Chelsea and Manchester City. The media interest would have been there."It's Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool that drive viewing figures, that drive clicks, that drive interest, that drive engagement."
Brand valueAnd that is the fundamental truth that drives so much frustration at Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool from City in particular, but also from those across the Premier League who share Cole's view. There may not be a Red Cartel, but it is hard to argue against the fact that those three teams are a bit different. Anyone who has worked in football media will be able to tell you that there is the web traffic generated by those teams and then, a chasm later, there is the rest of the league. You might not need that expertise either. Wherever in the world you are reading this, there is a fair chance you are more likely to cross paths with an Arsenal, Liverpool or Man United fan than a fan of any other team, with Chelsea as a potential exception. 
                                                                    Brand Finance
                                                            That much is apparent in Brand Finance's most recent assessment of the value of the world's top 50 football clubs. One might reasonably assume that City's perceived value to non-UAE sponsors has taken something of a kicking over the course of the last month. If that is the case, quite the gap has emerged between England's premium brands and the rest.Ultimately, these three clubs timed their ascent fortunately. Liverpool's success in the 1970s and 1980s was among the contributory factors in their popularity in continental Europe, particularly Scandinavia, as indeed it was among floating voters in the UK. The establishment of the Premier League as a global sporting mega league dovetailed with Arsene Wenger, Sir Alex Ferguson, Thierry Henry and David Beckham duking it out for titles. It's no wonder so many felt compelled to pick a side in that great rivalry. And once you've picked your team, you're probably stuck with it. This isn't a grocery store.
These teams aren't willing to settle for what they have. Kevin Demoff, president of team and media operations at Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, has suggested that "Arsenal can be the biggest global brand in the world." The Gunners, who have worked deliberately to situate themselves at the nexus of culture and creativity since being fully taken over by the Kroenkes in 2018, are the yardstick by which the rest of the KSE empire is assessed, Demoff added. That is a collection of sports teams that includes the Denver Nuggets, Los Angeles Rams and now the Los Angeles Angels. Against all those teams, many of them championship winners, it is the team from north London that is considered the most premium brand.Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have the weight of history in their favor. Sponsors want their reflected glow. Players dream of taking the field at the Emirates, Anfield and Old Trafford. Managers convince themselves they are the one to turn the project around. Can anything be done about that? The rest of the Premier League could drag them into a more balanced playing field in financial terms.Maguire's pitch is a hard cap based on average player costs with a "super tax." "What the owner has to do is put the additional cash in an escrow account. If the owner walks away or if their business goes belly up then you've got three years' worth of physical cash to acclimatise to a different lifestyle." Even he acknowledges that it's a hard sell. "Liverpool aren't going to vote for it because it increases competition. Brighton aren't going to vote for it because [owner] Tony Bloom doesn't have enough money to compete with Newcastle and Aston Villa."
Proposals for an anchoring system, which would have limited spending on squad costs to five times the broadcast and prize money of the league's bottom club and might have included a salary cap, were summarily dismissed when put to a vote in November 2025. Seven clubs voted in favor of the proposals. Manchester City were among those to vote against.Realistically, even balancing out the money only does so much. If the English top flight were to implement the sort of financial regulations more commonly associated with the NBA or NFL, Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United would still be the premium franchises. Their resonance, their location, their history would attract the best in much the same way as the Los Angeles Lakers or Miami Heat do. However you organize a competition, there is no escaping the fact that some teams are just bigger deals than others.Given the opportunity to hamstring the richest teams, the Premier League, in which television revenue is still distributed more equitably than in many other major European leagues, continually chooses not to. That, of course, is the point. If ever the other 17 clubs deemed the imagined cabal to be over-mighty, they could bring it to heel swiftly under the "tyranny of the majority" that was Manchester City's issue when they were fighting the league over associated party transactions. It would seem quite a challenge to run the Premier League from the shadows when you have less than half the votes required to block any changes.And so no, there is no Red Cartel. But then you, I and Manchester City probably knew that already.

title: Canelo Alvarez vs.Christian Mbilli fight predictions, odds, expert picks, undercard - CBS Sports
description: The former undisputed champion looks to regain a title on Halloween night
body:
The former undisputed champion looks to regain a title on Halloween night

        On Saturday, Saul "Canelo" Alvarez will enter the ring in the rare position of world title challenger. Alvarez will face WBC super middleweight champion Christian Mbilli in Saudi Arabia in Alvarez's first fight since September 2025.In Alvarez's previous fight, he suffered the most humbling defeat of his professional career, dropping a clear decision to Terence Crawford. Crawford was the much better fighter that night, using his world-class skills to beat Alvarez to the punch and constantly disrupt his rhythm.Unlike Alvarez's prior losses, he was not the far more inexperienced fighter facing a hall of famer (like against Floyd Mayweather Jr.) or the smaller man coming up in weight against a pound-for-pound elite (as was the case against Dmitry Bivol). Alvarez was younger than Crawford with a history of huge fights and Crawford was moving up multiple weight classes for the mega-payday of facing Canelo.What happened against Crawford seemed to validate all the doubts that had built up over the years. Alvarez has a ton of in-ring miles on his body at 36 and has seemed to have lost a few steps in recent years. Plus, Alvarez has not scored a stoppage since 2021. Time seemed to be catching up to Alvarez, and against a fighter as skilled as Crawford, there was no escape for the then-undisputed champion.

        
            
                Why the time is now for Canelo Alvarez to prove that he still has it on the elite, championship level
                
                    Brian Campbell                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Those doubts, and the question of how much Alvarez has left in the tank, lead us to Saturday and Mbilli, who was promoted from interim to full champion when Crawford retired following his win over Alvarez.Mbilli is a hard-charging fighter who has yet to taste defeat in his professional career, putting up a 29-0-1 pro record with 24 knockouts.Mbilli won the WBC interim belt with a first-round knockout of Maciej Sulecki, the second first-round knockout in a three-fight span for Mbilli. His first defense of the interim belt came against Lester Martínez on the undercard of Alvarez's fight with Crawford.
Against Martinez, Mbilli was on his usual game early, coming forward, throwing big right hands and working the body, but he fatigued down the stretch, which has been a recurring problem for the muscular Mbilli. The result of the fight was a very competitive draw that could have realistically gone either direction.Mbilli vs. Alvarez fight card, oddsSaul "Canelo" Alvarez -330 vs. Christian Mbilli (c) +250, WBC super middleweight titleJaime Munguia -1800 vs. Nikita Zon +850, super middleweightsRafael Espinoza (c) -3000 vs. Ricardo Blandon +1100, WBO featherweight titleDavid Picasso -700 vs. Carl Jammes Martin +450, featherweightsReito Tsutsumi vs. Raymundo Rojas Garcia, junior lightweightsPredictionWere you to design a fighter in a lab who is most tailor-made for peak Alvarez, he'd look a lot like Mbilli. Mbilli doesn't have a deep bag of tricks, he comes forward and he throws big combinations with good body work. Mbilli doesn't have solid defense, and he has shown a tendency to fade as fights wear on. Add to those problems that Mbilli has only been scheduled for a 12-round fight once (his first-round knockout win over Sulecki), and you can see the areas that Alvarez has clear advantages.The biggest question for the fight is what Alvarez has left in the tank. He has spent more than two decades fighting at a professional level. There are no mountains really left to be conquered for Alvarez, and he has shown that, even if still great, he is well past his prime as a fighter.
But has Alvarez faded enough that a simple pressure fighter -- even a good one -- able to break him down and collect a win?It seems unlikely that Alvarez can't lean on his skills, defense and boxing IQ to roll through Mbilli on the scorecards. Mbilli leaves too many defensive openings and doesn't have the game to disrupt Alvarez the way Crawford did repeatedly. Alvarez should leave the ring as world champion once again. Pick: Saul "Canelo" Alvarez via UD

title: What happened to Bryce Young and the Panthers' passing game? - CBS Sports
description: The last time the Carolina Panthers appeared in primetime, Bryce Young threw for 329 yards and two touchdowns in a 32-26 win over the Li
body:
The last time the Carolina Panthers appeared in primetime, Bryce Young threw for 329 yards and two touchdowns in a 32-26 win over the Lions. Young was both efficient and impressive, hitting on all the new, creative solutions offensive coordinator Brad Idzik had installed and making some big-time throws needed. An 18-yard sideline dart to Tetairoa McMillan on a third and 14 late in the game epitomized everything that was going right for the Panthers' passing offense, led by a massive step by Young.By the end of the night, Young was leading the NFL in passing yards.But that was then, and this is now. After a 27-19 loss to the Packers, the Panthers are 3-4 and have produced back-to-back offensive stinkers. Just four days earlier, they were blown out 43-13 by the Buccaneers, a game in which Young threw two interceptions and took five sacks. Thursday, Young took six sacks and threw a pick.Teams have bad games and even bad stretches. But this stretch has been particularly worrisome for the Panthers for a bevy of reasons: Young's play, yes, but also a crumbling offensive line and opponents figuring out some of Idzik's and Young's tendencies. Given Young's rocky career path thus far, there are big questions arising, the same big questions that have followed him his entire career. Do the Panthers have answers?Problem No. 1: The offensive line has fallen apartYoung's biggest strength has always been his mind. He is terrific at dissecting defenses both pre- and post-snap. This week was always going to be a challenge. Short weeks on the road leave far less time to prepare, and it often becomes a "players, not plays" scenario when it comes to determining a winner; physical skill wins out.
Young, because of some of his physical limitations, has a thin margin for error. And when the Panthers trot out an offensive line like this, especially against a blitz-heavy, disguise-heavy Packers defense, that margin for error completely disappears.Panthers' ideal OLPanthers' OL ThursdayReasonLT Ikem EkwonuLT Rasheed WalkerEkwonu is injured (torn patellar tendon)LG Damien LewisLG Corey BullockLewis is injured (knee)C Luke FortnerC Luke FortnerN/ARG Robert HuntRG Robert HuntN/ART Taylor MotonRT Monroe FreelingMoton is injured (broken leg/ankle)This group doesn't cut it. Walker was particularly brutal, allowing four pressures and a sack and committing two penalties. Fortner and Freeling allowed three pressures, and Hunt allowed two. In fact, the only players who didn't allow a pressure, according to PFF, were Bullock (who left early with an injury) and Jake Curhan, who was called up from the practice squad.Injuries have completely destroyed this unit. The Panthers knew they'd be without Ekwonu for most of, if not all of, this season. Walker was supposed to be a suitable replacement. He had been an established starter for the Packers. Instead, his 30 pressures allowed are the most in the NFL.At the other tackle spot, Moton has been a steady presence for years. But he missed the start of the year with blood clots and then broke his leg and suffered ankle ligament damage that ended his season after two games. Freeling, a first-round pick who was viewed as a project and is coming off a knee injury, has played a ton. He currently ranks 65th out of 71 tackles in PFF's grades (Walker is tied for 58th).On Thursday, Amazon Prime commentators Kirk Herbstreit and Al Michaels discussed the Panthers trying to "protect" their tackles. But really, there was nowhere to hide and, for Young, nowhere to escape. What is he supposed to do when three offensive linemen -- including both tackles -- get beat immediately?
Or when Freeling gets beat so easily it's like he was hardly there?
The tackles are far from the only problem. Fortner has given up 18 pressures, six more than any other center. The left guard spot currently belongs to Bullock, who only joined Carolina after not surviving the Ravens' final cuts.As such, Young has faced the ...most pressures in the league (133)most quick pressures in the NFL (80)highest pressure rate when not blitzed (45%), on pace for the highest rate since 2023 Justin Fieldsfifth-highest pressure rate overall (45%)fourth-most hits in the NFL (50)That's impossible to survive. While he isn't faultless for his sack problems, PFF says the offensive line has been at least partially responsible on 83% of the pressures he's faced, the 10th-highest rate in the NFL.Problem No. 2: The easy solutions are gonePerhaps the play most illustrative of this problem was actually one of Young's better plays Thursday. On an RPO throw, Young nearly ripped it to Tetairoa McMillan immediately. The problem? Packers linebacker Ty'Ron Hopper was standing right there. He knew what was coming. Young double-clutched, McMillan worked his way into a tiny sliver of space, and Young fired for a first down.Still, it showed that one of the solutions Idzik implemented this offseason, these quick-hitting passes, are getting more challenging and less effective.Bryce Young -- Passes under 2.5 secondsWeeks 1-5Weeks 6-8Success rate54.5%41.7%EPA per play0.40-0.16TD-Int4-02-2When you're trying to protect your offensive line, quick throws make sense. But an over-reliance on them makes them too easy to defend. Young threw 20 passes that came out in 2.5 seconds or faster Thursday, the most of the season, and his 40% success rate on these throws was his worst of the season.Problem 3: Defenses closing in on Young, who isn't 100%Smart opponents are basically saying, "Want to beat us over the top? Prove it." Two of Young's worst games this year have been against the Browns and the Packers, who rank first and third, respectively, in press coverage snaps. The other was against the Buccaneers, who knew they didn't need to press or blitz because they were constantly wreaking havoc up front (42% pressure rate) even without doing so.There's a game plan here to compress everything in front of Young and see if he can win deep, which he can't under current conditions. Thursday, Young went 1 for 6 on passes 10+ yards downfield and only attempted one pass 20+ yards downfield.Bryce Young this seasonvs. CLE, TB, GBvs. everyone elseEPA per dropback-0.250.25Negative play rate14.7%6.0%Net yards per attempt4.97.9Completions 10+ yards downfield1134Using net yards per attempt, Young is on par with Daniel Jones and Jalon Daniels in those three bad games and on par with Drake Maye and Trevor Lawrence in every other game.The problem? Teams are starting to pick up on the weaknesses.Young was ninth in net yards per attempt through six weeks (7.4). He's averaging 4.5 net yards per attempt over the past two weeks.Another problem? Young isn't 100%. He's been on the injury report with a knee issue the past several weeks, and though he hasn't missed any practice time, coach Dave Canales thinks it's impacting him."I would say that he certainly doesn't look like he's got that quick, make you miss type of deal, but he was able to create some space for himself," Canales said, per the team's transcript.Young's sack rate and sack-to-pressure rate are way up, indicators of a lack of protection and a lack of escapability. Opponents will attack each and every weakness relentlessly, and right now, both Young and Carolina have many.Can the Panthers turn it around?The short answer is yes, but the ceiling is low.
If it feels like every week is a referendum on Young, it's because he walks such a fine line between success and failure. He is not going to overcome suboptimal surroundings consistently. He is very smart and accurate in tight spaces when not under pressure, but he is rarely going to win deep, and his arm-strength issues prevent him from accessing all areas of the field. That's why it feels like defenses are closing in so much. They are challenging Young to win in places he doesn't usually win.The line has to get better for Young to have any chance. Canales is confident it will."I just think it comes down to a protection plan deal for us, because when we give Bryce time he's shown his ability to be able to spread the ball around, distribute it, find accurate throws in traffic and all those things, and I'm confident if we shore that thing up, which we will -- when we shore that part up -- Bryce will be back in his rhythm making the throws that he can."Idzik will come up with some solutions, too, and a mini-bye here should help. But we've seen throughout Young's career that the ceiling is relatively low. Even at his best, he's a middle-of-the-league quarterback, and those "at his best" stretches are fragile. That much is clearly and obviously on display right now.

title: NBA's five biggest X-Factors for 2026-27 season: Hopes hinge on Joel Embiid, LaMelo Ball and others - CBS Sports
description: These five players are the major swing pieces that could shape the new NBA season
body:
These five players are the major swing pieces that could shape the new NBA season

        The most important players of a given NBA season are the best ones. Shocker. The 2027 NBA champion will probably hinge first and foremost on the Victor Wembanyamas and Shai Gilgeous-Alexanders of the world. We know they're great. It's not as though the stars cancel each other out, but we take their greatness as a given and make predictions accordingly. Where our predictions are usually wrong, though, is a tier or two down.A reserve becomes a starter. A starter becomes an All-Star. An All-Star becomes a legend. Someone, or multiple someones, vastly outperforms expectations in a way that pushes his team over the top. These are the X-Factors of a given season, the players whose development or fit or health has a chance to turn a contender into a champion. We've now seen a week of games in the 2026-27 season, and these are the players who stand out as the major swing pieces in the 2027 championship race.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    1. Ajay Mitchell, ThunderThe Oklahoma City Thunder gave 11 players at least 900 minutes last season. Five of those players, due to either trade or injury, are either gone or should not be expected to return this season. The Thunder preemptively replaced Isaiah Joe with Jared McCain in a move that now looks brilliant. The addition of Aday Mara deepens the front-court enough to potentially offset some of the lost wing depth, like Aaron Wiggins.The defensive losses of Lu Dort and Cason Wallace are substantial. The same is true for Jalen Williams, perhaps more than either, because of his size. Still, the Thunder have an incredible collection of rim-protectors, and they still have Alex Caruso, who can guard anyone on the planet. They'll be able to find a wing defender on the trade market if they want to. Whether it's someone like Derrick Jones Jr. on the lower end or Herb Jones on the pricier one, adding defense is doable given their available assets and salary circumstances.

        
            
                What Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace injuries mean for the Thunder and why a trade isn't so simple
                
                    Sam Quinn                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
But replacing Williams-level shot-creation is a much, much taller order, and unless the Thunder are willing to put an amount of draft capital on the table that we can't presently foresee, it's going to have to come internally. The Thunder had no path to good shots against the Spurs last season with Williams and Ajay Mitchell hurt. The offense became mostly contested Shai Gilgeous-Alexander mid-rangers in that series, with a dash of hot shooting from Caruso and McCain barely keeping them afloat.For now, Mitchell remains healthy, and his volume has soared since Williams went down. The Thunder, for now, will likely treat him as their No. 2 option. The mid-range scoring is there. The finishing and the pull-up shooting -- both necessities for advantage creation against Victor Wembanyama -- have to improve. Mitchell has already grown plenty in two NBA seasons, and the opportunity now in front of him is a tremendous one. He's drawn Jalen Brunson comparisons for the past year. Well... who just slayed Wembanyama in the Finals? Mitchell has a ways to go before he can live up to a name that lofty, but he flashed future stardom in the first two rounds of Oklahoma City's run a year ago. That's where he'll have to go if the Thunder are going to avenge last year's loss to San Antonio.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    2. Ivica Zubac, PacersIvica Zubac had 15 rebounds on opening night. Do you remember the last time Myles Turner had 15 rebounds in a game? November 2021. Six years ago. For players with relatively similar levels of career accomplishment, you may not find two players who differ so much stylistically at the same position. The Indiana Pacers won the East with five-out spacing and all of the offensive advantages that came with it. Indiana no longer has that. They've traded it in for, well, everything else.
He's the far sturdier defender at this point. Rebounding is, well, something new for Indiana out of its centers. Zubac is a stronger screener and passer than Turner, and he's a more capable interior scorer as well. Figuring out how to integrate all of those skills without letting his lack of 3-point shooting get in the way of everything they already had is going to be a process, and early injuries to both Zubac and Tyrese Haliburton will slow that process.Zubac and Haliburton have only played 52 minutes together, but the early returns here are positive. It can be hard to find a place to stick non-shooting bigs when two other players run pick-and-roll, but Haliburton's ability to draw two to the ball and Pascal Siakam's ability to attack basically any coverage balances the court comfortably enough for Zubac to feast from the dunker's spot.
When Zubac is screening in these actions, his passing against 4-on-3s fits Indiana should almost always lead to good looks.
The Brooklyn Nets and New Orleans Pelicans in October are hardly the sort of defenses Indiana should expect to see when it counts, but the Pacers will dial up the offensive sophistication as the comfort here grows. For now, everyone is just getting to know each other, but if the Pacers can figure out how to take advantage of all of the new things Zubac brings to the table, their offense is going to be even more diverse for this playoff run than it was in 2025.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    3. LaMelo Ball, TimberwolvesThe Charlotte Hornets didn't think LaMelo Ball could be their franchise player. The Minnesota Timberwolves didn't need him to be. Putting him next to Anthony Edwards would theoretically amplify the best elements of his game and sand down some of its edges. You don't have to take as many circus shots or try the sort of audacious things that lead to turnovers that Ball has been doing forever when defenses are fixated mostly on someone else. In small doses, those things lead to the sort of "giddiness" that Chris Finch has welcomed. In more concentrated form, well, you get unserious basketball, the sort Charlotte is trying to get away from.That's what makes this early Edwards injury so enormous for Minnesota. It's not just the absence of his productivity. It's the fact that this is a relatively new and young team still figuring out its identity, and the last team that had Ball decided that the foibles that come with building everything around him were not an identity they wanted to try to sustain. Minnesota looked great in its first four games with Ball and Edwards together. 
Ball was dreadful in his first solo star outing, finishing with nearly as many turnovers (6) as he had points (8). His best season in Charlotte, a year ago, came after the arrival of Kon Knueppel and the emergence of Brandon Miller. Before the Hornets could actually support him, well, things were uglier.That's not exactly exclusive to Ball, but it's the fear Minnesota is facing now. The Timberwolves are deeper than the Hornets teams Ball grew up with, but there's no Knueppel or Miller around anymore. For better or worse, he is going to fully define the next few months of Minnesota's season, and finding the balance between the things that make him special and the things that Charlotte was afraid made him expendable is going to be tricky considering just how much Minnesota now needs out of him. The stakes here are high. Oklahoma City's injuries create vulnerability atop this conference in a way that may not exist in a year. It's hard to imagine Minnesota taking advantage of that from the Play-In Tournament, so winning regular-season games while Edwards is out really matters. Doing so in a way that doesn't compromise the identity of the team Edwards comes back to matters more. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    4. Alperen Sengun, RocketsOne of the biggest storylines of the 2026 playoffs were the specific ways a handful of centers bothered Wembanyama. Very, very few bigs can genuinely do it offensively. Isaiah Hartenstein did so with his parabolic floater. Karl-Anthony Towns did so with his combination of shooting and driving. The Spurs, with Oklahoma City compromised, are the measuring stick right now. And something we're reminded of every time the Houston Rockets face San Antonio is how much Alperen Sengun seems to relish the challenge of attacking the NBA's best defender.
Sengun shot 17 of 23 with Wembanyama as his primary defender last season, according to NBA.com tracking data. He just posted a 29-point, seven-assist game against Wembanyama a week ago. He has a notable strength advantage over the Defensive Player of the Year, and his game is starting to round out in such a way that he poses many of the problems Towns did, albeit in different ways. He doesn't have a Hartenstein-level floater, but it's good enough and arcs high enough to force Wembanyama to step away from the rim to try to contest it, which in turn opens up the paint for Sengun as a passer. He's starting to take 3s again too, though we'll see how long that lasts. A year ago, Sengun took 3.4 3s per game in his first 11 appearances and more or less stopped from there. With Fred VanVleet and Steven Adams back, it's probably a skill Sengun leans into a bit more this season, and it's another spot on the floor that Wembanyama has to respect.Having some sort of answer to the Wembanyama question is a contention prerequisite moving forward. You may not be able to neutralize him completely, but you have to find a way to render him defensively mortal. There are only a handful of bigs in the NBA that can do that. Houston may have one of them, and if that's indeed the case, with the Thunder hobbled, they are probably the single Western Conference team best suited to unseating San Antonio and reaching the Finals.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    5. Joel Embiid, 76ersThey may share a uniform, but Joel Embiid and the rest of the Philadelphia 76ers often look as though they play for different teams. Everyone else in the starting lineup and most of the bench wants to run. Between the outlet passing of LeBron James, Jaylen Brown's ability to punish the wrong cross-matches and the sheer athleticism of Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe, Philadelphia should be among the best transition offenses in the NBA. They rank 27th in transition frequency and 21st in transition efficiency, according to Cleaning the Glass. This isn't just an Embiid problem, but he sticks out like a sore thumb in this respect.This is by no means an insurmountable stylistic clash. Remember, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar played center for the Showtime Lakers. The ability to modulate pace can be a lethal weapon, and Embiid remains a very effective player. Thus far, he's just not the sort of effective center who makes sense on this specific roster. Individual shot-creation is plentiful here. Someone bouncier, someone who uses fewer possessions and makes quicker decisions, probably fits a bit better here. Too bad. Embiid is on a three-year, super max contract that figures to be very difficult to trade. You don't always get the ideal stylistic fit. You make do with what you have.He's made some concessions on this front. He's holding the ball almost a full second less per possession than he did a year ago. He's in good shape, moving better than he is in years... though still far from where he'll need to be against offenses that can put him in the blender as the New York Knicks did a year ago. He remains an effective rim-protector defensively, though he's closer to a stationary one. It's far too early to judge Philadelphia's defense as a whole. The on-off numbers are deceptive because of how limited Embiid's backups are and how absurdly lucky they've thus far gotten on opponents' 3-pointers when he's played.
It's not as though 2020 Anthony Davis is walking through that door (even if 2026-27 Davis is a popular fake trade target). Embiid is mostly who he is, and the Sixers are going to have to find ways to blend what he does best with what their four other starters actually need out of a center. It'd be nice if he started making his 3s again, a problem that has now persisted several seasons. This is one way the speed disparity here could be beneficial: trailer 3s. His shooting just about everywhere has been down thus far, and that's going to have to correct itself if he's going to justify his volume.The theory of this roster was less about a specific style than sheer, overwhelming talent. The idea here is that Philadelphia can generate advantages and mismatches so easily with so many high-level players on the floor that even a version of the team that isn't optimized can be great. That's a lot easier in October than in May. Finding the synergies between these very different sorts of players will be the entire point of this regular season for the 76ers.

title: MLB qualifying offer: Predicting who will get a QO this offseason, plus how the $23.15 million contract works - CBS Sports
description: It's unclear how -- or if -- the new CBA will change the QO system, which could leave teams more hesitant to make
body:
It's unclear how -- or if -- the new CBA will change the QO system, which could leave teams more hesitant to make an offer this winter
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 30, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:27 am ET
                        
                •
            
            8 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Milwaukee Brewers have been crowned the 2026 World Series champions and the 2026-27 offseason is    already underway. More than 100 players became free agents the day after  the  World Series ended, and soon teams will have to make decisions  about  contract options and  qualifying offers.    The     qualifying offer (QO) entitles teams to draft-pick compensation in the    event that they  lose a free agent to another team. The QO is a one-year deal    set at the  average of the top 125 salaries in baseball. This    offseason, it's worth a record $23.15 million, according to the New York Post. That is up from $22.025 million last year, $21.05 million the year before, and $20.325 million the year before that.    Teams    have until five days  after the end of the World Series to   tender  their free agents the QO,  and players who receive it then have until 4  p.m. ET on Nov. 17 to  accept or reject. Players who accept   the QO  remain with their team and cannot be traded without their consent until June 15. Players who reject the QO become free agents with  draft-pick compensation attached.     Simple, right? The process is, but  the   decisions aren't always. With  that in mind, let's run down this offseason's QO candidates, as well as explain the draft-pick compensation rules.    
Does the QO still apply this offseason?    Yes, the QO is still a thing this offseason. The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the next CBA could change the QO rules, maybe even eliminate it entirely. That said, until that happens, the QO remains in place. Decisions to tender the QO (made by the team) and decisions to accept or reject the QO (made by the player) are due before the CBA expires.        Compensation rules    Once upon a time, teams that lost  an eligible free agent received a    compensation draft pick after the  first round. It was nice and easy.   The  current rules are a bit more  complicated. Here are compensation   rules  for teams that lose a  qualified free agent:          Former teamContract sizeCompensation 2027 draft pickReceived revenue sharing 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Less than $50 million 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round) 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Received revenue sharing 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$50 million or more 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Pick after first round 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Paid competitive balance tax 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				N/A 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Pick after fourth round 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				All other teams 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				N/A 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round) 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				The Athletics, Brewers, Cardinals, Diamondbacks, Guardians, Mariners, Marlins, Orioles, Pirates, Rays, Reds, Rockies, Royals, Tigers, and Twins received revenue sharing this season, so the first two scenarios apply to them. The Blue Jays, Braves, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, Red Sox, and Yankees will pay competitive balance tax (CBT), so they're in the third scenario. The Angels, Astros, Giants, Nationals, Rangers, and White Sox neither received revenue sharing nor paid CBT. They're in the fourth bucket.   Now here are the penalties for signing a qualified free agent:    Signing team2026 draft pick forfeited2027 international bonus money forfeitedPaid CBT 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Second- and fifth-highest 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$1 million 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Received revenue sharing 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Third-highest 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				none 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				All other teams 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				Second-highest 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				$500,000 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				 				The Blue Jays, Braves, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, Red Sox, and Yankees   will pay CBT and are in the first group. The Athletics, Brewers, Cardinals, Diamondbacks, Guardians, Mariners, Marlins, Orioles, Pirates, Rays, Reds, Rockies, Royals, Tigers, and Twins received revenue sharing and are in the second group. The Angels, Astros, Giants, Nationals, Rangers, and White Sox are the third group. Got it? Good.  Thirteen players received the QO last offseason: Trent Grisham, Shota Imanaga, Gleyber Torres, and Brandon Woodruff accepted the QO; Zac Gallen, Michael King, and Kyle Schwarber declined but signed new contracts to remain with their teams;  Bo Bichette, Dylan Cease, Edwin Díaz, Kyle Tucker, Ranger Suárez, and Framber Valdez rejected the QO and signed with new teams, giving their former clubs compensatory draft picks. Teams do not gain or lose draft picks for re-signing their own qualified free agent.    Not eligible to receive the QO  Players are eligible for the QO as long as they spent the entire 2026 season with one team and did not receive the QO previously. That means several high-profile free agents are not eligible for the QO this offseason. Here are the notables:  CHANGED TEAMS  Luis Arraez  Kevin Gausman (also received QO previously)  Casey Mize  Freddy Peralta  Tarik Skubal  Daulton Varsho  PREVIOUSLY RECEIVED QO  Bo Bichette (opt out)  Sonny Gray (mutual option)  Michael King (opt out)   Nick Martinez  The Tigers traded Skubal, the reigning two-time AL Cy Young winner, to the Dodgers for a three-prospect package at the deadline. MLB Pipeline currently ranks those players as Detroit's No. 1 (Zyhir Hope), No. 3 (River Ryan), and No. 9 (Brady Smith) prospects. That's a much better haul than the compensation draft pick the Tigers would have received had they kept Skubal all year and made him the QO. Anyway, these free agents are among those not eligible for the QO this offseason.    Locks to receive the QO  This is not the best free agent class and, as a result, I count only two stone-cold locks to receive a QO: Randy Arozarena (Mariners) and Seiya Suzuki (Cubs). The Mariners and Cubs would be thrilled if Arozarena and Seiya accepted the QO and returned next season on one-year contracts that aren't too much of a raise. Arozarena made $15.65 million this year. Suzuki earned $18 million. The jump to $23.15 million isn't big enough to shy away from the QO, plus these are really good players. Arozarena and Suzuki will receive the QO and decline it.    Likely to receive the QO  Although Arozarena and Suzuki are the only locks to get the QO, in my opinion, there are three other free agents-to-be who seem like pretty good bets to receive it. Here are those three players:  
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Ryan Jeffers, Twins: Jeffers will be the best catcher to hit the open market since Willson Contreras four years ago. He missed time with a hamate injury this year and his defense isn't great, plus he'll turn 30 next June. Those seem like nitpicks compared to the offense he brings to the table at the catcher position. The only reason I don't think Jeffers is a lock to get the QO is the fact that the Twins have shaved roughly $50 million off their payroll the last four years. They might get thrifty.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Brandon Lowe, Pirates: Pittsburgh knocked it out of the park with the Mike Burrows-for-Lowe-and-Mason Montgomery three-team trade with the Astros and Rays. Montgomery is a bullpen ace and Lowe slugged 35 home runs, the most by a Pirate since Josh Bell hit 37 in 2019. Lowe's age (32), poor contact rates, and history of poor defense (though not in 2026) create collapse risk. Also, the Pirates run a bottom 10 payroll every season. I expect Lowe to get the QO. I just wouldn't be surprised if the Pirates decide not to risk him taking it, thereby soaking up 20% or so of their 2027 payroll.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Trevor Rogers, Orioles: Rogers, 29 in November, was a bright spot in an otherwise lost season for the O's. He stayed healthy and threw a career-high 169 ⅔ innings, and pitched exceptionally well after June 1: 2.90 ERA with under-the-hood numbers to match (2.89 FIP and 3.10 expected ERA). Rogers might be the second-best free agent starter behind Skubal given his success the last two years and (more importantly) analytically friendly arsenal. During the president of baseball operations Mike Elias era, the Orioles haven't always done the most sensible thing when it comes to spending money. I think it's 99% certain the O's will give Rogers the QO, but 99% is not 100%.  
  On the bubble  My hunch is teams will be conservative with their QO decisions this offseason because a new CBA is coming, and no one knows what the game's economic landscape will look like next year. Will there be a salary cap? More punitive CBT penalties? I would expect teams to err on the side of caution when it comes to potentially committing $23.15 million to one player. Even a good player they may want back, but not necessarily at $23.15 million in 2027. Here are three borderline QO cases:
                            
    
                                                
                    
    David Bednar, Yankees: Bednar has proven he can close games in New York, which is not nothing, but he did just turn 32, and the $23.15 million QO would make him the highest-paid reliever in baseball. I think the Yankees want to bring Bednar back next season. Enough to risk him accepting the QO? When the potential reward is a dinky draft pick after the fourth round given their CBT status? That I'm not sold on. A multi-year contract at a lower annual salary is the much more likely path to Bednar returning to the Yankees.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Jazz Chisholm Jr., Yankees: Even in a down year, Chisholm was a 3.5-WAR player thanks to the breadth of his skill set. He hit 19 homers, he stole 41 bases, and he was fourth among second basemen with +13 outs above average. The all-around game and the fact that Chisholm will play the entire 2027 season at age 29 would seem to make him a slam dunk QO candidate. My sense is the Yankees won't commit any significant payroll to next season without first seeing what the new CBA brings, which is exactly what they did before the last lockout. I think the Yankees value the payroll flexibility (i.e. the certainty that Chisholm won't take the QO) more than the post-fourth round compensation pick they would receive if he signed elsewhere.  
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Adrian Morejon, Padres: Morejon will be an interesting test case for San Diego's new ownership. He is outstanding, one of the five or six best relievers in baseball, and he'll play the entire 2027 season at age 28. The QO would make Morejon the highest-paid reliever in the game, but only if he takes it, and his age and effectiveness would seem to make that unlikely. Do the Padres roll the dice and give Morejon the QO, and risk sinking $23.15 million into a (great) setup man, or not bother because they're only in line to receive a draft pick after the fourth round if he leaves? Díaz, Josh Hader (from the Padres), and Raisel Iglesias are the only relievers to get the QO in the last seven years. Is Morejon in that class?

title: NFL Week 8 schedule: Why you should watch these three underrated games - CBS Sports
description: Here are three games you should watch that people may not be talking about
body:
Here are three games you should watch that people may not be talking about
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 30, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:12 am ET

            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        It's Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season, and this is just about the time when the window for teams' playoff possibilities starts to close. We saw some significant results last week, both good and bad.The Texans losing another and falling to 2-5 raises questions about whether their season is done for. The Seahawks had a very redeeming win, handing the Chiefs their first loss of the season in a blowout. Staying in that division, the Rams made things interesting in the standings by getting a check in the win column as well. The Falcons also kept their season hopes trending positive by handing the 49ers their first loss of the season.This all just proves that even if a team isn't on the top of the playoff picture, their games may end up being the most interesting ones of the week.Which brings us to why we are here: it's time for the weekly edition of underrated NFL games. Here are three games you should keep on your radar: 
Chargers vs. RamsSunday, Nov. 1 at 4:05 p.m. ET on Fox (Stream: Fubo -- try for free)It's the battle of the Los Angeles teams this week, and it always adds an interesting layer when squads who share a stadium face each other. While they both call SoFi home, one team does have to be dubbed the home team and this time it's the Rams, meaning the Chargers will have the visiting locker room in their own stadium.The Chargers are basically playing for the No. 1 seed at this point. No NFL team has ever started the season 0-6 and made the playoffs. The worst start for a team that ended up in the postseason was by the 1992 San Diego Chargers, who went 0-4 and finished 11-5.Head coach Jim Harbaugh is on the hot seat and needs to get his team looking somewhat better if he wants to keep his job, and 0-7 doesn't look great to front offices.
The Rams are also not off to the best start, though it seems amazing compared to their Week 8 opponent. There are many 3-4 teams in the league that are in the playoffs, and Super Bowl chances seem slim, but that's not the case for the Rams. Despite their wildly underwhelming start, they still have the fifth-best odds of winning the Super Bowl (+1100), per DraftKings Sportsbook. If they fall to the no-win Chargers, however, those odds may plummet. This is a big game for both teams, as one looks to avoid going 0-7 and the other fights to reach .500.Patriots vs. Dolphins Sunday, Nov. 1 at 4:25 p.m. ET on CBS, streaming on Paramount+We know how much I love divisional games, because they are the most unpredictable, have the most history and carry the most weight. The Dolphins are 1-5, so this likely won't affect the final divisional standings between these two teams, but it could have a significant impact elsewhere.
The Patriots could still win the AFC East, though they are behind the Bills, they did win their first head-to-head against Buffalo. New England retook their AFC East throne last year, after a few years of the Bills getting that hat and t-shirt feeling when Tom Brady left. If the records are close down the line, these divisional games will mean a lot, and right now the Patriots need that boost.The other interesting thing about this game is that, even though the Patriots are on paper a better team in every category, they historically struggle in Miami. The Patriots have lost five of their last six games in Miami. Will the Patriots lose to the Dolphins? Most likely not, but it could get closer than people think; divisional games tend to do that.  The Patriots are looking to bounce back from a 30-24 loss against the Chicago Bears. They beat themselves in the game numerous times and an easier opponent will be a good test of whether they can correct those mistakes and look dominant enough to be a threat in the AFC.
Falcons vs. Buccaneers Sunday, Nov. 1 at 1 p.m. on Fox (Stream: Fubo -- try for free)The NFC South includes the 3-3 Panthers, 3-4 Atlanta Falcons, 2-5 Buccaneers and 2-5 Saints. This game will likely have significant implications for the divisional rankings. This is also a matchup between two teams who struggled in the beginning of the year and have found a resurgence. The similarities don't end there; both teams had quarterbacks sidelined for multiple weeks, with the Falcons' Michael Penix Jr. sidelined while recovering from an ACL injury and the Bucs' Baker Mayfield sidelined due to a thumb injury.The Falcons are coming off a huge win against the San Francisco 49ers, handing them their first win. The Bucs are coming off a win against the Panthers. I think these teams will have a lot of fight in them this week and it will make for a very competitive game.

        The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only two days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Bichette picks up player option 
As expected, Mets infielder Bo Bichette has picked up his $42 million player option for 2027, reports The Athletic. He holds another $42 million player option for 2028. Still only 28, Bichette had a poor first season in Queens, posting a .702 OPS with 18 home runs while showing growing pains as he transitioned from shortstop over to third base. For now, the Mets are set on the infield with Bichette at third, Francisco Lindor at short, and Marcus Semien at second. They must figure out first base, and it is possible they will make a trade to shake up that veteran infield. Moving Semien would be ideal, but it may not be doable. Lindor's name figures to pop up in trade rumors against this offseason. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
     D-backs will listen to offers for Marte 
The Diamondbacks are expected to listen to offers for second baseman Ketel Marte, reports the Arizona Republic. The D-backs entertained trade offers last offseason, but were unable to find a match. Marte has full no-trade protection and can direct where he lands, if he wants to leave Arizona at all. His desire to change teams is unknown. 
Marte, 33, had a down year by his standards in 2026. He also went AWOL in August, prompting the D-backs to put him on the restricted list. Manager Torey Lovullo later revealed it was the fourth straight season Marte missed a game without permission. Beyond the on-field fit, teams will have to weigh the potential clubhouse impact and headaches.  Seibu Lions will post Taira The Seibu Lions in Japan will make right-hander Kaima Taira available to MLB teams via the posting system this offseason, the team announced Friday. The posting is expected to be made official in the coming days. Once that happens, Taira will have 45 days to negotiate and sign with an MLB team, otherwise he will return to Japan in 2027. We ranked Taira as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason. Here's our write-up: 
Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. 	Taira, 27 next month, threw 146 innings with a 1.36 ERA and 141 strikeouts this past season. He actually had higher ERAs as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, though he has been excellent throughout his career in Japan, and has the bat-missing power stuff that tends to translate well to MLB. Taira figures to be highly sought after in the coming weeks. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Red Sox make two minor trades 
The trading season resumed Thursday and the Red Sox were involved in the offseason's first two trades. First, they sent utility man Nate Eaton to the Athletics for minor-league righty Jareth Rayo, the team announced. The A's recently named former Red Sox assistant general manager Taylor Smith their new president of baseball operations. His first move was bringing in Eaton, a player he's presumably familiar with given their overlapping time in Boston. Next, the Red Sox traded infielder Tsung-Che Cheng to the Tigers for cash, the team announced. Cheng, 25, is a glove-first utility man who appeared in 14 games with Boston this past season. Both the Cheng and Eaton trades open up 40-man roster spots for the Red Sox, who still must open three more spots to accommodate their seven players on the 60-day injured list. They must be activated no later than this coming Monday.

In advance of last season, six different people who type words about college basketball for CBS Sports were asked to predict the winner of the 2026 NCAA Tournament. We gave six different answers. Regardless of whether things were actually that wide-open or not, the fact that six different schools could reasonably be picked suggests it felt that way at the time. But this time around the replies were much more focused. Some were Florida. Some were Duke. Nobody else got a so-called first-place vote. If we're right, that means either Florida's Todd Golden is about to win his second national championship and basically solidify a spot in the Naismith Memorial Hall of Fame or Duke's Jon Scheyer is about to get his first after winning a record 124 games in his first four years as a head coach.Full Final Four predictions from our experts are below.
        
            
                2027 NCAA Tournament Bracketology: Duke No. 1 in preseason projections, expansion puts squeeze on mid-majors
                
                    David Cobb                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
 Bold predictions for 2026-27 season  Cinderella is dead George Mason, FAU, Loyola Chicago and Butler are among the true mid-majors that have advanced to a Final Four this century. Add it up, and five mid-majors made the Final Four from 2006 to 2013. That's five in an eight-year span. Based on where things are headed, I believe those days are over. So my bold prediction is that not only will zero mid-majors make the 2027 Final Four, I'm ready to suggest we won't see one again for the next decade. The gap between the haves and have-nots is just too big now to think a team built on a mid-major budget, a budget that is probably overwhelmed by nearly power-conference team in the bracket, if not every power-conference team in the bracket, can really win four games over a two-week span against that kind of competition. — Gary Parrish  Freshman of the Year comes from the Big 12, but it isn't Tyran Stokes It will be 6-foot-5 Arizona wing Caleb Holt, who I expect to average better than 15.0 points, 7.0 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 1.5 steals for the Wildcats this season. But it will be his defensive prowess will be what gets Holt past the likes of Stokes (Kansas), Jordan Smith Jr. (Arkansas), Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje (Duke), Jason Crowe Jr. (Missouri) and Bruce Branch III (BYU). 
My prediction also factors in Arizona beating out Kansas for the Big 12 title, which could tilt some of the accolades in his honor. Boumtje Boumtje's ceiling is crazy-high, but he's got the most talent around him; he'll be the preseason NPOY favorite 12 months from now. Holt is going to be incredible and narrowly win out in what I think will be a fabulous marathon for the nation's top frosh. — Matt Norlander  An SEC team one game above .500 will make the NCAA Tournament Auburn nearly crashed the party last season after arriving at Selection Sunday with a 17-16 record. This time around, someone with a similar record will make the field from the SEC. The NCAA Tournament's expansion from 68 to 76 teams almost guarantees it. The league is projected to be a dominant force, which means most conference games will fall into Quad 1 or Quad 2. As such, SEC losses won't be particularly penal in Bracketology metrics. An SEC team with a 6-12 league record might even get a look, so long as they performed reasonably well in nonconference play. This isn't going to sit well with the anti-expansionists, but teams at or just barely above .500 will routinely be part of the bubble conversation in this new era. — David Cobb
        
            
                United States of College Basketball: Ranking the best team in each state for the 2026-27 season
                
                    Matt Norlander                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
 Unlikely Duke star earns player of the year  Duke has an abundance of riches because this is the deepest roster in the sport. The Blue Devils have had back-to-back player of the year winners (Cooper Flagg and Cameron Boozer), and my bold prediction is that streak will continue. However, it won't be John Blackwell, who was voted a preseason All-American by CBS Sports. It will be 17-year-old freshman sensation Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje. The 7-foot-2 forward will make an impact on both ends of the floor. I'm confident that at some point this season, he will be Duke's best player. That should give him a chance to win the top individual honor in the sport. — Cameron Salerno 
 St. John's takes next step St. John's has the best backcourt in the sport. Point guard Quinn Ellis, shooting guard Ian Jackson and slashing wing Tounde Yessoufou form a devastating trio. Ellis' creation, Jackson's shooting and Yessoufou's drives mesh together perfectly. There is no positional overlap here at all, and the talent jumps off the tape. Jackson and Yessoufou are both former five-star prospects who now get to play with an unselfish, set-the-table point guard like Ellis who just wants to create good shots time and time again.  Ellis plays like he's a 23-year-old vet who played against ex-NBA players in the EuroLeague last year probably because he's a 23-year-old vet who played against ex-NBA players in the EuroLeague last year.  This caliber of point guard play should allow Jackson and Yessoufou to be the best version of themselves. Rick Pitino's backcourt is primed to shred. — Isaac Trotter

     Duke  The Blue Devils get their first national title in 12 years — and do so cathartically after two legendary melts in 2025 and 2026. Jon Scheyer may not have a national player of the year on this roster, but Duke probably has the most talent of any team. That was true of the past two years as well, of course. It just might be time for the Blue Devils to break through. Those defeats to Houston and Connecticut calloused Scheyer; he can learn from them. Duke didn't lose a game by more than three points last season and brings back four significant minutes-eaters (Pat Ngongba, Caleb Foster, Dame Sarr, Cayden Boozer) in addition to maybe the No. 1 draft pick in 2028 (Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje) and one of the five best transfers of 2026 (John Blackwell).  I think Duke wins the title, but more than that, makes history as the first men's team to win at least 35 games in three consecutive seasons. This is in part a function of having longer schedules in the past 25 years than they had up until the mid-'90s, but three straight seasons with at least 35 victories would be outrageous. — MN 
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Florida As I've written many times in the Top 25 And 1, where Florida has been sitting at No. 1 for most of the offseason, on paper, the Gators are the obvious pick to win the 2027 NCAA Tournament. They're returning six of the top seven scorers from a team that won the sport's best conference (SEC) by three games last season while securing a No. 1 seed in the 2026 NCAA Tournament. Yes, Iowa ultimately ended the Gators' season in the Round of 32. Regardless, that Florida team was great and likely will be again. 
Remember how Michigan's entire frontcourt was selected in the first round of the 2026 NBA Draft after winning the 2026 NCAA Tournament? The same thing could happen at Florida, where Thomas Haugh, Alex Condon and Ruben Chinyelu represent college basketball's best 3-4-5 combo Haugh, specifically, is the SEC's Preseason Player of the Year after averaging 17.1 points and 6.1 rebounds last season while shooting 46% from the field. — GP
