 Other predicted Final Four teams 
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Texas Tech  At full strength, Texas Tech is one of the best teams in the country. Of course, this prediction hinges on two things happening: JT Toppin coming back and playing at an All-American level off an ACL tear, and Donovan Atwell, Darrion Williams and Jamichael Stillwell being eligible to play. If both happen, I feel very confident that Texas Tech will overachieve based on expectations. The additions of Cruz Davis and Dra Gibbs-Lawhorn out of the transfer portal should also serve the Red Raiders well. Texas Tech came close to reaching the Final Four in 2025 before losing to eventual national champion Florida. This season, Texas Tech returns to the final weekend of the season. — CS 
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Illinois Illinois is beginning the season a little banged up. But it's not how you start, it's how you finish. With four of the top 100 And 1 players, including CBS Sports preseason first-team All-American David Mirkovic, the Illini are poised to follow up their 2026 Final Four run with a repeat trip. Five players from last year's rotation are back, including the towering Ivisic brothers and wing Andrej Stojakovic, who shined in the NCAA Tournament. Between those three and Mirkovic, Illinois will again tower over the opposition. While guards Kylan Boswell and Keaton Wagler are gone, coach Brad Underwood landed high-caliber replacements. Five-star freshman Quentin Coleman and Providence transfer Stefan Vaaks are the headliners of the overhauled back court.  Coleman was great during Illinois' exhibition slate. Three-star freshman Ethan Brown is going to make an impact, too, and will help keep the floor spaced as a great shooter. This program got a taste of the big stage last April, and it's got every ingredient needed to get there again. — DC

                            
    
                                                
                    
     Arkansas This is John Calipari's deepest roster since he took over at Arkansas. Last season's roster was full of talent, but lacked depth. That won't be an issue this season. The lone returner from last season's team is Billy Richmond III, who should have an expanded role on the offensive end of the floor this season. Richmond is one of the most athletic players in the sport and is entertaining to watch on a nightly basis. So is Jordan Smith Jr., who projects as the latest star one-and-done guard Calipari will coach. The other names to watch: JJ Andrews, Abdou Toure and Miikka Muurinen. — CS
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Miami Miami is going to knock some teams out, literally and figuratively. This team is built to play smashmouth basketball, and that's just the way Jai Lucas wants it. Miami can trot out some enormous lineups with Shelton Henderson (6-6, 239 pounds), Caleb Gaskins (6-8, 221 pounds), Malik Reneau (6-9, 245 pounds) and Somto Cyril (6-11, 263 pounds) all on the floor together. That should be an elite rebounding group that dominates the paint on both ends. Oh, and it has one of the best point guards in the sport. Acaden Lewis is a basketball savant. The Villanova transfer is a paint-touch machine who plays with a ton of creativity, both as a scorer and as a creator. Miami needs Reneau to stay eligible all year long in the 5-in-5 fiasco, but this roster is just loaded size and high-pedigree recruits. If Miami can get just enough shooting from Gaskins, Lewis, sophomore guard Dante Allen or someone off the bench like Nick Dorn or Brent Bland, Miami is going to be in business. — IT

        
            
                2026-27 College Basketball Preseason All-Transfer Team: Louisville's Flory Bidunga is top player out of portal
                
                    Isaac Trotter                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    

                            
    
                                                
                    
     UConn Dan Hurley was recently voted college basketball's best coach by a panel of writers and analysts at CBS Sports. If this season unfolds the way I assume, he'll do nothing to hurt his professional standing this season and will coach in the Final Four for what would be a fourth time in a five-year span. In any era, that would be amazing. In this era, where the transfer portal is constantly giving and taking, it would be even more so.The Huskies are fourth in the Associated Press Preseason Top 25 poll, same as they are in the Top 25 And 1. Silas Demary and Braylon Mullins are the backcourt stars. They combined to average 22.1 points, 8.0 rebounds and 7.3 assists last season while helping the Huskies advance to the title game of the 2026 NCAA Tournament. Presumably, only one of them will win Big East Player of the Year honors -- but either could. — GP
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Texas The only double-digit seed to reach the Sweet 16 in March follows it up with the first Final Four strut of Sean Miller's career. I wrote this earlier in the offseason, but the one team that looks the most similar in 2026 to how eventual champion Michigan was built in 2025? Texas. Miller loaded up with five high-end transfers, led by former Colorado guard Isaiah Johnson (16.9 ppg) and former TCU forward David Punch (14.1 ppg). I'm going UT to the Four in part because I think Matas Vokietaitis (15.6 ppg) makes the leap. Texas ranked top-10 in offseason spending; this is one of Sean Miller's best teams, at least on paper.  The Horns, like Duke, have a 17-year-old on the roster who projects as a top-five pick 19 months from now. Marcus Spears Jr. will get an initiation into college ball a year ahead of pace after reclassifying in the summer. He's a great bonus developmental piece to bring into a squad that was already firmed up at every position and not hurting for depth. I think Texas finishes second to Florida in the SEC and both make their way to Detroit. — MN  

                            
    
                                                
                    
     Virginia Backing teams with awesome bigs is a shrewd preseason strategy. Virginia has just that, and a whole lot more. Burly Belgian Thijs De Ridder is one of the elite power forwards in the sport who can smash mismatches and drain 3-pointers. 7-foot German center Johann Grunloh could be one of the breakout bigs in the ACC because he impacts the game in so many ways. Sophomore guard Chance Mallory is one of the easiest breakout picks on the board after grading out in the 79th percentile in pick-and-roll efficiency. Sam Lewis is the fourth starter back, and the 6-7 wing is a total baller who can score at all three levels and owns a devastating handle, to boot. Virginia's four returners get well-deserved buzz, but Ryan Odom made sharp additions. German 24-year-old Nolan Adekunle shot 43% from 3 and 71% at the rim in Germany's top professional league last year. The physical wing is slated to start at the 3 for UVa. Jurian Dixon, Elijah Gertrude and Christian Harmon are all real-deal snipers that Odom can bring off the bench.  Frankly, Virginia would be getting way more buzz if it didn't lose a nip-and-tuck, second-round game to Tennessee last March. The amount of size, skill and shooting on this roster, surrounding a stud point guard like Mallory, forms a recipe that can win elimination games. There's just not a lot of holes on this roster. — IT 
 NCAA Tournament surprises Teams not in the AP Top 25 who will advance to second weekend of NCAA Tournament 
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Purdue Braden Smith, Trey Kaufman-Renn, Fletcher Loyer and Oscar Cluff were Purdue's top four scorers last season. They combined to average 53.2 points per contest. But now they're all gone. So, after five straight top-15 finishes at KenPom, the computers and human rankings are expecting the Boilermakers to slip. That's why they're unranked in the preseason AP poll. But anybody who listens to the Eye On College Basketball Podcast regularly understands that I'm a program-truster in the sense that I usually assume winning programs will continue to win as long as the coach and culture remains in place. That's not always true, of course. But giving certain coaches and programs the benefit of the double is often wise, and that's what I'm doing here in predicting that unranked Purdue will, one way or another, make the Sweet 16 next March for what would be the fifth time in a six-year span. — GP
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Ohio State The Buckeyes were a No. 8 seed last season and got better in the spring, giving Jake Diebler a real shot at finishing in the top five of the Big Ten and earned a No. 6 seed or better in 2027. OSU was the highest-ranked team in my Top 100 And 1 rankings not to earn an AP preseason slot. The 3-point shooting of John Mobley Jr. (41.1%), the scoring talent of five-star freshman Anthony Thompson and the do-it-all ceiling of the most underrated sophomore in America, Amare Bynum, should have OSU in a position to make its first Sweet 16 since 2013. — MN 

        
            
                Ranking college basketball coaches: UConn's Dan Hurley tops Houston's Kelvin Sampson, St. John's Rick Pitino
                
                    David Cobb                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    

                            
    
                                                
                    
    MarquetteMarquette is poised for a bounce-back season after a rare down year under sixth-year coach Shaka Smart. The Golden Eagles return star guard Nigel James Jr, and Smart has shown more willingness to use the portal. St. Thomas transfer Noah Minessale and Louisville transfer Sananda Fru help raise the floor. Whether you look at KenPom, Torvik or EvanMiya, you'll find Marquette rated as a top-35 team entering the year. Fru should be especially helpful on the rebounding front after Marquette got killed on the glass last season. — DC
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Missouri Missouri is a team I'm surprised wasn't ranked in the initial preseason AP Top 25 poll. This is one of the more talented rosters in the SEC, headlined by five-star guard Jason Crowe Jr. If you want another bold prediction: Crowe will be a top-three scorer in the SEC this season. He's that good. If the Tigers can get Mark Mitchell eligible to play, this is a team that can finish top-five in the SEC and make a deep NCAA Tournament run. I like the roster that Dennis Gates has assembled. This is the year Missouri gets out of the first weekend for the first time since 2009. — CS
                            
    
                                                
                    
     Iowa Losing an All-American and first-round point guard like Bennett Stirtz has helped Iowa fly under the radar a little bit in the preseason hype machine. Ben McCollum has another really good team hiding in plain sight. This Hawkeyes frontcourt could be outstanding. Saint Mary's transfer Andrew McKeever is a total load at 7-3. He can single-handedly help Iowa go from an OK rebounding team to a great board-cleaning unit. His gravity as a roller and his comfort as a playmaker should help Iowa's offense pick defenses apart with sharp cutters and deadeye shooters. Big wings like Cooper Koch and Tate Sage are net-shredders from downtown, and McCollum is an incubator for player development. It wouldn't surprise me at all if some of these returners like Kael Combs or Trevin Jirak have another gear it can get to. This is also a bet on McCollum's brilliance in single-elimination games coming to life yet again. He forces the game to be played on his terms. McCollum was a dominant single-elimination coach at the Division II level, and that's already carried over at Drake (4-1) and Iowa (4-2). Iowa will be very pesky because its frontcourt is way better this year, but its ceiling rises even more if speedy Illinois State transfer point guard Ty'Reek Coleman turns into a sparkplug by the time March rolls around. I genuinely believe Iowa could be even better than last year because it's way bigger and has more shooting. — IT

title: Cam Skattebo says he feared amputation after gruesome injury that ended his 2025 season - CBS Sports
description: In a new documentary about his recovery, he also said he had a pregame premonition about his injury
body:
In a new documentary about his recovery, he also said he had a pregame premonition about his injury
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 30, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:46 am ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo is coming off his best game of the season, having rushed 17 times for 124 yards and a touchdown against the Houston Texans last week. Skattebo had been unceremoniously benched in the previous game, taking just six snaps and recording zero carries following a costly fumble the week before, so it was good to see him get back to form.Early in the season, Skattebo was running extremely inefficiently and averaged just 3.6 yards per carry over the Giants' first five games. That was perhaps unsurprising when you consider that his 2025 season ended with a right ankle dislocation, an open tibia fracture and a ruptured deltoid ligament. That's a scary injury, and one that can obviously affect a running back's performance, given how important cutting and changing direction are to succeeding at the position.Skattebo said earlier this year that he had considered retirement in the wake of the injury, and this week he and the Giants released an hour-long documentary detailing his recovery. He revealed more about his situation, including that he was afraid his foot would have to be amputated and that he had a premonition about a potential injury before the game."Before the game, I actually had an out-of-body experience," Skattebo said, via GiantsWire. "We were all praying in the showers. I was holding both my teammates' hands. It almost felt like, when we were praying, my body was lifted out of my own body. It was weird. I didn't feel like I was in the present me. I didn't feel like myself."
Once he saw what the injury looked like, he feared doctors would have to amputate his foot."When I first got hurt, like I'm asking the doctors, like, they're going to have to cut my foot off," he said, via The New York Post."As soon as the doctor touched my foot, I felt pain. He snapped (my ankle) back into place, and it was like, 'A sigh of relief.' Once I got in the X-Ray room, they cut my shoe off, they cut my sock off, I was a half-second from passing out because I had dislocated it so far that the skin ripped."
Skattebo obviously did not get his foot amputated and did not retire, and is now back on the field and looks like the lead back for the Giants — especially after the team cut Najee Harris and placed Tyrone Tracy Jr. on injured reserve. He will need to maintain the improved efficiency he showed against the Texans, but just being back on the field and playing at all is pretty impressive considering the extent of the injury he sustained.

description: The former Roc Nation CEO will remain through January 2027 after stabilizing the conference with a new media righ
body:
The former Roc Nation CEO will remain through January 2027 after stabilizing the conference with a new media rights deal and eight expansion additions
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 30, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:11 am ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Big 12 commissioner Brett Yormark will step down from the conference office and take a job outside of college athletics, the league announced on Friday. Yormark is expected to be with the conference through Jan. 31, 2027. "Serving as the commissioner of the Big 12 Conference has been an extraordinary honor," Yormark said. "I want to thank the Big 12 Board of Directors, Board Chair Douglas A. Girod, athletic directors, coaches, student-athletes, fans, fellow commissioners and trusted colleagues at the league office. I am looking forward to passing the baton to the next commissioner and continuing to cheer their league on as a lifelong fan of the Big 12." Yormark stepped into the conference at a pivotal time in 2022 as the league faced a major realignment moment. He helped shepherd the league through adding eight new schools in a two-year period and negotiated a long-term television contract that stabilized the league. He was an unusual choice at the time after never working in college athletics, instead coming immediately from his role as CEO of Jay-Z's Roc Nation. He also worked in NASCAR and with the Brooklyn Nets. 
Under his leadership, the Big 12 vastly increased its business portfolio, including a partnership with Monster Energy to serve as naming rights partner on the football and basketball sides. The league also introduced a live music halftime show during the Big 12 Championship Game. The Big 12 now faces a pivotal hire heading into the back half of its television contract, with more realignment expected ahead of a 2031 contract date. Aggressive figureComing to the Big 12 from outside college sports, Yormark brought a unique mindset. Instead of leaning on stability, Yormark embraced the changing college athletics landscape and remade the league in his image. 
Former commissioner Bob Bowlsby previously added UCF, BYU, Houston and Cincinnati from the Group of Five level in the wake of Texas and Oklahoma leaving the league. However, Yormark was even more assertive. As both the Big 12 and Pac-12 negotiated television contracts, Yormark jumped in front, agreeing to terms with ESPN and FOX and boxing the Pac-12 out of the market. With the Pac-12 left with primarily streaming options, Yormark lobbied Colorado, Utah, Arizona, and Arizona State to defect from the league, ultimately leading to the conference's collapse. Heading into the last realignment, the Big 12 was long seen as the likeliest league to collapse. Because of Yormark's leadership, however, the league survived. 
There were times when Yormark's aggression led to some unpopular pushes. Yormark reportedly pushed UConn in realignment to cement power on the basketball side, and he repeatedly mentioned the idea of international games. However, his personality was a critical part of the Big 12 increasing its revenue after the loss of Texas and Oklahoma. Where does the league go?With Yormark's departure, the Big 12 is at a crossroads. The first four full-time commissioners of the league were typical hires from inside college athletics. Yormark was a major zag, even compared to other FBS commissioners. Now, the Big 12 is more financially and competitively stable. That leaves the conference with a wide swath of options from which to find their next commissioner. 
"I'm going in very open-minded," Kansas chancellor Doug Girod told ESPN. "I don't need a (Yormark) twin. I need someone who hopefully has some experience with campuses, and mostly is going to be an innovator and help us on that path of revenue diversification and thinking differently about how we conduct ourselves and be the tip of the spear in some of these changes."The SEC's Greg Sankey and ACC's Jim Phillips are both traditional commissioner candidates from the college athletics world. The Big Ten opted to go to the television world with Tony Petitti, a longtime television executive at CBS and with the MLB Network.

title: Meet Tom Nolan: The rising Aussie star looking to make a splash in his first main event - CBS Sports
description: Learn more about the burgeoning star ahead of his first UFC Fight Night main event against Renato Moicano
body:
Learn more about the burgeoning star ahead of his first UFC Fight Night main event against Renato Moicano
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 30, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:11 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Tom Nolan earned his first UFC main event the hard way. The Australian lightweight has become a legitimate contender in one of the promotion's deepest divisions, with a tenacious style and an unusually studious approach to his craft.Nolan (11-1) headlines UFC Fight Night against Renato Moicano on Saturday at the Meta APEX in Las Vegas. He's won four straight fights since losing his UFC debut, most recently upsetting Fares Ziam to break into the lightweight rankings. The 26-year-old now has the opportunity to establish himself against a veteran he's long revered, one who has shared the Octagon with some of the division's best.The matchup came together because Nolan was willing to step up. Moicano was originally scheduled to face Brian Ortega at UFC 332, but Ortega withdrew from the fight. Nolan offered to step in. Moicano had little interest in facing such a dangerous young opponent on short notice. Instead, Moicano said he advocated for a five-round main event to give both fighters proper time to prepare.Sign up for Paramount+ and watch UFC for no additional fee -- every UFC numbered event and UFC Fight Night is included with your subscription! Plans start as low as $8.99/month or $89.99/year!

        
            
                Why a childhood punch convinced Jacobe Smith he belonged in the UFC: 'It changed me'
                
                    Shakiel Mahjouri                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Ahead of the biggest fight of Nolan's career, let's get to know the rising Australian contender, from the fighters who shaped his style to the bully he knocked out on his way to the UFC.He's fighting one of his 'heroes' on SaturdayNolan was studying Moicano well before they were scheduled to meet. He dissected Moicano's dominant stoppage win over Benoit Saint Denis to prepare for another Frenchman, Ziam. One grappling sequence in particular caught Nolan's attention."The way he used the body triangle to go between mount and back mount. I just thought it was a beautiful way to keep his hips facing the floor at all times," Nolan told CBS Sports. "There are only a few examples of it at a really high level to study, and you know, I'm a big believer in keeping up with the times and studying the sport."
Nolan was 14 when Moicano made his UFC debut, submitting Tom Niinimaki in the second round. He's long admired Moicano's ambitious fighting style, calling him "one of the heroes" he watched growing up. Moicano, however, isn't interested in a touching idols-becoming-rivals narrative."F--- that, Tom Nolan," Moicano told reporters at Wednesday's Media Day. "I'm gonna beat your f---ing ass, bro. Stop that shit. I don't want compliments, I want money."Fortunately, Nolan's admiration isn't subduing him. The best way to honor his hero is to beat him with some of Moicano's signature techniques.
"Ground and pound. Some elbows would be very nice. Just slicing and dicing would be sick," Nolan said. "He's very good at that. I'd love to do that to him."
He took Fares Ziam's lightweight rankingKnowledgeable fans recognized that Ziam vs. Nolan was excellent matchmaking, even though oddsmakers had favored Ziam considerably. Their June 6 fight justified the excitement. The lightweights fought for three hard rounds, with Nolan landing twice as many significant strikes and holding his own in several grappling exchanges.Nolan walked away with a unanimous decision win and Ziam's spot in the Top 15. It was an especially convincing win because Ziam looked like a legitimate threat to the lightweight elite. Afterward, Ziam downplayed the loss, claiming he lacked fire and focus. Nolan wasn't surprised.
"I picked up on that vibe when I met him," Nolan said. "I thought he would be a little bit like that after losing. People have different personality types. Everyone needs to find a reason why they lost. I think the best guys in the world and the champions can always look internally and say, 'OK, what did I do wrong?' That's what I do with my loss. I completely blame myself. I don't want to make excuses. I have to learn from this and be better. I think other people don't do that."The Quillan Salkilld conundrumBeating Moicano brings Nolan closer to an awkward reality. His friend and fellow Australian prospect Salkilld is creating a buzz in the same division. Salkilld is scheduled to headline his second consecutive UFC Fight Night on Feb. 7, facing Saint Denis in Australia. Nolan and Salkilld don't train at the same gym, but Australia's MMA scene is remarkably collaborative. Rivalries between major camps aren't uncommon elsewhere, such as the famous feud between Florida's American Top Team and the Blackzilians. Australian fighters, meanwhile, freely exchange knowledge and train together despite representing different gyms.Nolan and Salkilld have discussed possibly fighting each other, but Nolan believes there are enough opportunities for both men to succeed without crossing paths in the Octagon.
"We've spoken about it. We're boys, we're on the come up. I think we're both big enough that whoever wins the title could go up, but I don't know. It's not really something I think about. I'd prefer not to fight any Anzacs," Nolan said, referencing Australian and New Zealand fighters. "I love the homies back home. We started on this scene as underdogs, just a handful of us. Now we're really starting to take over. I love the idea of all of us pushing together and beating everyone up."Cory Sandhagen assisted his 'Contender Series' KONolan was a UFC fan long before he became a UFC fighter. Two of his favorite fighters, Charles Oliveira and Cory Sandhagen, underscore that with their technically sophisticated yet fan-friendly styles. Nolan has a similar appetite for striking, outlanding nearly every opponent he's fought. But his appreciation for Sandhagen reaches far past the Octagon."I think Cory Sandhagen is one of the greatest technicians in the sport, and his striking understanding is at the highest level," Nolan explained in a UFC Q&A. "I also think he has a huge portion of his mental growth as a person and an athlete on display in his interviews and instructionals, which is really important for the sport to show how we evolve as the years go on.
Nolan's studious approach predates his fights with Ziam or Moicano. Ahead of his "Contender Series" debut, Nolan contacted Sandhagen for advice. The two exchanged messages, and Nolan made Sandhagen a promise."I messaged him and said, 'Hey, when are you putting out your flying knee knockout [instructional video]? How do you set this up? How did you do this?' We went back and forth. I said to him, 'I'm flying on 'Contender Series' in two weeks, and I'm going to knock this dude out with one of your techniques.' And I actually used the dart shot that he teaches in an instructional, so I was like, 'Wow, that's insane."Nolan and Sandhagen make a good student-teacher combo. Nolan convincingly demonstrated what he learned from Sandhagen's instruction, knocking out Bogdan Grad in 83 seconds. UFC commentator Paul Felder described the finish as one of "the most deadly shots I've seen in a long time." 
UFC CEO and president Dana White had high hopes for Nolan when he awarded him a contract, calling him a "straight killer" with a bright future. "Only 23 years old," White said. "The only thing I have to say about this kid is you have a bright future, Tom Nolan."
He shut up a bully for goodNolan doesn't like bullies. He spent enough time dealing with them as a child, so knocking out Grad felt especially good.
Grad devoted weeks to antagonizing Nolan before their "Contender Series" fight. He bombarded Nolan with social notifications, sent bizarre flexing videos and issued ominous warnings about Nolan's fighting future. Nolan had been on the receiving end of similar treatment growing up, but now had the means to address it."It was a moment of growth for me to realize, oh wow, I did exactly what you've just described," Nolan said.Nolan takes greater satisfaction in what happened afterward. Grad returned to the "Contender Series" one year later to secure a UFC contract. He's coming off a win in August, but Nolan barely recognizes the man he knocked out. 
"The coolest thing is that guy is now in the UFC, and his whole approach is complete humility," Nolan said. "It's like it humbled him and changed him. So that's probably my proudest part about it, to be honest. I turned him from a bully into a reasonably good guy, which is cool. He's having a lot of success in the UFC now.

        We've made it to Week 9 of the college football season, and conference races are really starting to heat up. This weekend will create some separation with key games in the Big Ten, Big 12 and SEC.The day starts with a huge Big 12 clash between No. 22 Arizona and No. 13 Texas Tech. The Red Raiders are coming off their first loss of the season, and the Wildcats are rolling. The pressure is on Texas Tech to get back on track, and Arizona is looking to prove itself against the best teams in the conference after losing to BYU earlier in the fall. The Wildcats at least have the quarterback edge with Noah Fifita playing at a high level.In the afternoon, No. 3 Georgia plays No. 17 Florida in the World's Largest Indoor (?) Cocktail Party. Both rivals are coming off an open date, but their last games couldn't have been more different. Georgia was knocked off its No. 1 perch by Auburn, and Florida pulled off an upset against Texas. Will either of those results carry over to this game?Elsewhere, No. 25 Wisconsin's trip to Iowa City will have major implications on the Big Ten race to the College Football Playoff, and No. 2 Ohio State goes to USC in what will be a major test for Lincoln Riley.
With so much football on at once, we've made a handy guide so you can prioritize your viewing experience.The best gamesNo. 22 Arizona at No. 13 Texas Tech -- 12 p.m. on ESPN, Fubo (try for free): The Red Raiders can't afford two consecutive losses, but here come the Wildcats with an upset on their minds. The vibes between these programs couldn't be any more different. Texas Tech super booster Cody Campbell is tweeting through it and threatening to restrict access for a local radio station. Meanwhile, Arizona coach Brent Brennan is buying shots for students after a blowout win over Iowa State. Unfortunately for the Wildcats, vibes alone don't win football games, and the Red Raiders will be desperate for a win.No. 25 Wisconsin at Iowa -- 12 p.m. on Fox, Fubo (try for free): One week has really flipped the outlook on this Big Ten matchup. Wisconsin went from unranked to No. 25 following a big ranked win over USC, and the Badgers have all the momentum rolling into Iowa City. The Hawkeyes, on the other hand, lost the Floyd of Rosedale at the buzzer as Minnesota kicked its way to hog heaven. Now Iowa is unranked and looking to rebound by taking home the Heartland Trophy -- a giant brass bull. If you thought it couldn't get much more Big Ten than Minnesota vs. Iowa, strap in for this matchup on Saturday afternoon and watch these programs paint a masterpiece.
No. 17 Florida vs. No. 3 Georgia -- 3:30 p.m. on ABC, Fubo (try for free): Depending upon the status of the Mercedes-Benz Stadium roof, the World's Largest Outdoor Cocktail Party may be moving inside. What we know for sure is that this matchup has a lot of intrigue, with Florida coming off an enormous win over Texas and Georgia coming off a gut punch against Auburn. The biggest question about this rivalry matchup is what the Gators will do at quarterback. Sophomore Tramell Jones did enough to beat the Longhorns, but did he do enough to lock down the starting job over Aaron Philo, who struggled before suffering an injury? I would say you can't roll Jones out against an elite defense like Georgia, but he was fine against Texas.Minnesota at No. 4 Indiana -- 3:30 p.m. on CBS, CBSSports.com, Paramount+ Premium: The spread for this game is enormous, which suggests it could be a get-right spot for Indiana. That said, the Hoosiers haven't exactly cruised through Big Ten play. They needed overtime to beat Michigan last week, although that game was on the road against a great defense. Neither of those things will be a factor on Saturday. Minnesota is coming off a huge rivalry win against Iowa, and now it has to face the defending champs on the road. The Golden Gophers will have to get something out of their abysmal run game (100.1 yards per game) to pull off the upset.No. 6 Utah at Cincinnati -- 3:45 p.m. on ESPN, Fubo (try for free): Can the Bearcats do it again? One week after handing Texas Tech its first loss, Cincinnati can do the same thing to Utah, which just beat Houston in a dramatic top-25 matchup. Cincy had a ton of success on the ground against the Red Raiders as it ran for 255 yards, but that will be much tougher to pull off against the Utes. That's because Utah ranks eighth nationally in rush defense, and the Bearcats will be in trouble if they have to rely on JC French's arm all game.
 No. 2 Ohio State at USC -- 7:30 p.m. on NBC, Fubo (try for free): Lincoln Riley needs a big win in the worst way, and he's already lost to a backup quarterback once with Dylan Raiola carving up USC for most of that game against Oregon. The second-ranked Buckeyes will bring an inexperienced quarterback into L.A. Memorial Coliseum -- whether it's Luke Fahey or Tavien St. Clair. It's a prime opportunity for Riley to cool his seat and put his team in position for a run at the College Football Playoff. If USC loses, however, the pressure on Riley will be greater than ever. Jeremiah Smith can really strengthen his Heisman Trophy candidacy if he plays well without Julian Sayin in the lineup.Best of the restNo. 5 Notre Dame at Navy -- 12 p.m. on ABC, Fubo (try for free)Auburn at No. 12 Ole Miss -- 12:45 p.m. on SEC Network, Fubo (try for free)No. 20 Northwestern at Oregon -- 3:30 p.m. on PeacockVirginia at No. 14 Wake Forest -- 3:45 p.m. on ESPN2, Fubo (try for free)South Carolina at Oklahoma -- 4:15 p.m. on SEC Network, Fubo (try for free)Clemson at Florida State -- 7 p.m. on ACC Network, Fubo (try for free)No. 1 Miami at North Carolina -- 7:30 p.m. on ABC, Fubo (try for free)Texas State at No. 20 Boise State -- 10 p.m. on CW, Fubo (try for free)
